at elske.explanation: "At elske" means "to love". It is a strong word, kept mostly for people you truly care about: "Jeg elsker dig" (I love you). For things and activities, Danes usually say "Jeg kan godt lide" (I like) or "Jeg holder af" (I am fond of). Saying you "elsker" (love) pizza is possible, but it sounds playful.

sentence.da: Hun vil **elske** sine børn for evigt.
sentence.en: She will love her children forever.

forms.da: Jeg har et brev i e-Boks.
forms.en: I have a letter in e-Boks.

e-boks.explanation: "En e-Boks" means "an e-Boks", the digital mailbox where public offices, banks and companies send you letters.

sentence.da: Jeg har fået et brev i **e-Boks**.
sentence.en: I have received a letter in e-Boks.

efter.explanation: "Efter" means "after", for time and for order. It also appears in many phrases where English says "for": "lede efter" (look for), "spørge efter" (ask for) and "længes efter" (long for). When a full sentence follows, you need "efter at", as in "efter at jeg kom hjem" (after I came home).

sentence.da: Vi går en tur **efter** middagen.
sentence.en: We go for a walk after dinner.

egen.explanation: "Egen" means "own", and it goes with words like "min" (my) or "din" (your). It also stresses that something is yours alone: "mit eget værelse" (my own room).

sentence.da: Jeg låner ikke din bil, jeg har min **egen** bil.
sentence.en: I am not borrowing your car, I have my own car.

ekstra.explanation: "Ekstra" means "extra", more than what you already have. It can also make another word stronger, as in "ekstra god" (extra good).

sentence.da: Vi er fem, så vi skal have en **ekstra** stol.
sentence.en: We are five, so we need an extra chair.

eller.explanation: "Eller" means "or". At the end of a question, "eller?" asks for agreement, a bit like "right?" in English: "Du kommer, eller?" (You are coming, right?). With "enten" it means "either ... or": "enten te eller kaffe" (either tea or coffee).

sentence.da: Vil du have te **eller** kaffe?
sentence.en: Do you want tea or coffee?

forms.da: skynd dig, ellers kommer vi for sent
forms.en: hurry up, or else we will be late

ellers.explanation: "Ellers" means "otherwise" or "or else". It says what happens if something does not happen, and it can also mean "apart from that". Do not mix it up with "eller" (or), which joins two choices.

sentence.da: Tag en jakke på, **ellers** bliver du kold.
sentence.en: Put on a jacket, or else you will get cold.

elleve.explanation: "Elleve" means "eleven". The numbers go on with "tolv" (twelve), "tretten" (thirteen) and "fjorten" (fourteen).

sentence.da: Vi er ti, og nu kommer min bror, så vi er **elleve**.
sentence.en: There are ten of us, and now my brother is coming, so we are eleven.

en e-mail.explanation: "En e-mail" means "an email" and is written with a hyphen. In daily speech people often shorten it to "en mail". You say "at sende en e-mail" (to send an email) and "at modtage en e-mail" (to receive an email).

sentence.da: Jeg har sendt dig en **e-mail**.
sentence.en: I have sent you an email.

en eftermiddag.explanation: "En eftermiddag" means "an afternoon", the part of the day from lunch until evening. "Om eftermiddagen" means "in the afternoon" as a regular thing, and "i eftermiddag" means "this afternoon". The word is built from "efter" (after) and "middag" (midday).

sentence.da: Klokken fire er det **eftermiddag**.
sentence.en: At four o'clock it is afternoon.

en elefant.explanation: "En elefant" means "an elephant". It is spelled with "f" where English has "ph", and it sounds much like the English word.

sentence.da: En **elefant** er et meget stort dyr med en lang snabel.
sentence.en: An elephant is a very big animal with a long trunk.

en elev.explanation: "En elev" means "a pupil", a child or young person who goes to school. It can also mean a trainee or apprentice at a workplace. Adults who study at university are usually called "en studerende" (a student) rather than "elev".

sentence.da: Min søn er **elev** i tredje klasse.
sentence.en: My son is a pupil in third grade.

en elevator.explanation: "En elevator" means "an elevator". Danes also say "en lift" (a lift), and both are understood everywhere. You go "med elevatoren" (by the elevator) up or down. The stairs are "trappen" (the stairs).

sentence.da: Jeg bor på fjerde sal, og der er ingen **elevator**.
sentence.en: I live on the fourth floor, and there is no elevator.

en enkeltbillet.explanation: "En enkeltbillet" means "a one-way ticket", for a trip in only one direction. "Enkelt" means "single", so it is literally a single ticket. The opposite is "en returbillet" (a return ticket).

sentence.da: En **enkeltbillet** til København, tak.
sentence.en: A one-way ticket to Copenhagen, please.

en euro.explanation: "En euro" means "a euro", the money used in many European countries. After a number it usually stays the same: "ti euro" (ten euros). Danish money is "kroner" (crowns).

sentence.da: Det koster tyve **euro**.
sentence.en: It costs twenty euros.

end.explanation: "End" means "than" and compares two things: "Hun er højere end mig" (She is taller than me). It comes after words like "større" (bigger) or "bedre" (better). Do not use "som" (as, like) for "than". The "d" in "end" is not pronounced, so it sounds like "en" (a).

sentence.da: Han er ældre **end** mig.
sentence.en: He is older than me.

endnu.explanation: "Endnu" means "yet" or "still". "Ikke endnu" means "not yet": "Jeg er ikke færdig endnu" (I am not finished yet). Before a word like "bedre" it means "even": "endnu bedre" (even better). "Stadig" (still) is a close word for something that is still going on.

sentence.da: Jeg er ikke færdig **endnu**.
sentence.en: I am not finished yet.

eneste.explanation: "Eneste" means "only" or "single", as in "the only one". It normally comes after "den", "det" or "de" (the): "den eneste" for en-words, "det eneste" for et-words. Do not mix it up with "kun" (just, only): "Jeg har kun én bil" (I have only one car).

sentence.da: Det er den **eneste** bus i dag.
sentence.en: It is the only bus today.

forms.en: Come and visit me some day!

engang.explanation: "Engang" means "once" or "some day", for a time that is not clear. "Der var engang" (Once upon a time) is how fairy tales begin, and "Kom og besøg os engang" means "Come and visit us sometime". Do not mix it up with "en gang" (two words), which means "one time", as in "en gang om dagen" (once a day).

sentence.da: Jeg boede i Italien **engang**.
sentence.en: I once lived in Italy.

engelsk.explanation: "Engelsk" means "English", for the language and for things from England. As a school subject, say "Jeg har engelsk" (I have English, meaning an English lesson). Words for languages start with a small letter in Danish.

sentence.da: Hun er fra England og taler **engelsk**.
sentence.en: She is from England and speaks English.

england.explanation: "England" means "England" and is spelled like the English word. It is only one part of the United Kingdom; for Great Britain as a whole, say "Storbritannien" (Great Britain).

sentence.da: London er en stor by i **England**.
sentence.en: London is a big city in England.

enogtyve.explanation: "Enogtyve" means "twenty-one". It is literally "one-and-twenty": Danish says the ones first, so 22 is "toogtyve" (two-and-twenty) and 31 is "enogtredive" (one-and-thirty).

sentence.da: Min søn er **enogtyve** år.
sentence.en: My son is twenty-one years old.

forms.da: Enten i dag eller i morgen.
Enten er du med, eller også er du ikke.
forms.en: Either you are in, or you are not.

enten…eller.explanation: "Enten … eller" means "either … or" and offers two choices: "enten" comes before the first and "eller" before the second. Between two whole sentences, Danes often say "eller også" (or else) for the second part. "Både … og" (both … and) is the opposite idea: you take both.

sentence.da: Vi kan **enten** gå **eller** tage bussen.
sentence.en: We can either walk or take the bus.

er det ...?.explanation: "Er det ...?" means "is it ...?". Danish asks a question by putting "er" (is) first, with no extra word like "do": "Er det rigtigt?" (Is that right?). Fill the gap with whatever you want to ask about.

sentence.da: **Er det** langt herfra?
sentence.en: Is it far from here?

er du sikker?.explanation: "Er du sikker?" means "are you sure?". "Sikker" means "sure" or "safe". You can answer "Ja, helt sikker" (Yes, completely sure). To ask several people, say "Er I sikre?" (Are you all sure?).

sentence.da: **Er du sikker?** Det er en lang tur.
sentence.en: Are you sure? It is a long trip.

et efternavn.explanation: "Et efternavn" means "a last name", the family name you share with your family. It is made of "efter" (after) and "et navn" (a name).

sentence.da: Mit fornavn er Anna, og mit **efternavn** er Hansen.
sentence.en: My first name is Anna, and my last name is Hansen.

et efterår.explanation: "Et efterår" means "an autumn" (or "a fall" in American English), the season between summer and winter. It is made of "efter" (after) and "et år" (a year).

sentence.da: Det er **efterår**, og bladene falder af træerne.
sentence.en: It is autumn, and the leaves are falling from the trees.

et enkeltværelse.explanation: "Et enkeltværelse" means "a single room", a hotel room for one person. It is made of "enkelt" (single) and "et værelse" (a room). The matching word for two people is "et dobbeltværelse" (a double room).

sentence.da: Jeg rejser alene, så jeg vil gerne have et **enkeltværelse**.
sentence.en: I am travelling alone, so I would like a single room.

europa.explanation: "Europa" means "Europe". It is written with a capital letter, as in English, and has no word like "the" in front of it. "Europæisk" means "European", and a person from Europe is "en europæer".

sentence.da: Frankrig, Italien og Danmark ligger i **Europa**.
sentence.en: France, Italy and Denmark are in Europe.

europæisk.explanation: "Europæisk" means "European". Unlike in English it is written with a small letter, except inside a name like "Den Europæiske Union" (the European Union). A European person is "en europæer".

sentence.da: Danmark er et **europæisk** land.
sentence.en: Denmark is a European country.
